newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers say bill will protect elderly.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers say bill will protect elderly.

text.p: A bipartisan coalition of lawmakers on Tuesday unveiled a bill to add new consumer protections to "Medigap" insurance policies that most senior citizens use to supplement federal Medicare health coverage.

The measure, sponsored by Rhode Island Republican Sen. John Chafee, West Virginia Democrat Jay Rockefeller and others, would bar insurers from setting waiting periods for new Medicare recipients who have pre-existing health conditions.
It would make it easier for disabled individuals who are eligible for Medicare to get Medigap policies, aiding an estimated 5 million people.
Continuously insured Medicare beneficiaries who enrolled in managed care plans, then decided during their first year they wanted to quit, would be guaranteed entry into a Medigap plan.
Further, the bill would guarantee continuously covered individuals could get a comparable policy if their Medigap plan went broke, they moved or lost their retiree health benefits.
"I believe that this Medigap bill could become one of the really crucial pieces of health care legislation which will pass in this Congress," Chafee told a news conference.
The bill also includes a $35 million grant for consumer education efforts.
The bill tracks some of the Medicare reforms included in the five-year balanced budget plan President Clinton sent to Congress last week.
About 38 million Americans are now covered by Medicare and about 80 percent of them have Medigap policies that cover prescription drugs and other out-of-pocket expenses not covered by Medicare.
An insurance industry spokesman predicted the legislation would force carriers to raise premiums, possibly putting Medigap policies out of the reach of some seniors.

"While the legislation certainly is well intended, we think that ultimately it will result in higher premiums and, therefore, could force seniors to drop or not purchase this important coverage," said Richard Coorsh, spokesman for the Health Insurance Association of America.
